issues.description: The submitted solution did not fix the observed failing case and therefore does not meet the acceptance criteria CA-01 and CA-02. The code is identical to the originally defective implementation and still returns 7 for input [1,6,4,3,2] instead of the expected 11.

The implemented greedy strategy (sort ascending and add any reward > current total) is incorrect for the problem. Including a smaller reward can make later larger rewards ineligible, so always taking every reward that is > current total is not optimal (example: [1,6,4,3,2] — the greedy picks lead to 7 but optimal is 11). A correct approach needs to consider subset feasibility: you can pick each value at most once and you must choose a subset whose elements can be ordered so each element is greater than the running sum. A practical correct implementation is to reduce duplicates (at most one instance of each value can be used) and use a DP/bitset approach over achievable sums (e.g., maintain a bitset of reachable totals and for each value v update new = (bits & ((1<<v)-1)) << v, then bits |= new). The current code does not implement this.

No tests or example-driven unit tests were provided in the workspace. There are no automated tests that assert the failing case from the task (CA-02) or other edge cases (small n, all-equal values, max constraints). Absence of tests makes regressions and verification harder.

The file contains the platform's preloaded imports region (not part of the solution) and then the solution body. The solution is a single small method which is fine for this task; however the greedy logic mixes decision and selection in a single pass which is the source of the bug. Also note that duplicate reward values cannot be chosen more than once in a valid sequence, so sorting and deduplicating before DP simplifies the state space.
